A constraint in longevity research: aging lacks a clear regulatory pathway. And since all-cause mortality trials for aging are unfeasible - every drug, even those born from aging research, will be tested against a specific disease instead. Because of this bottleneck, the next major milestones for the field are expected in three directions: Path 1: Win disease by disease. Show that a single drug succeeds in separate trials across several age-related diseases, making it hard to deny the drug is acting on aging itself rather than any one condition. Path 2: Test against multiple diseases at once. Successfully test a single drug against several age-related diseases simultaneously in a single trial, directly demonstrating that it acts on aging broadly. Path 3: Change the rules. Get a regulator to approve new trial designs based on surrogate endpoints using functional parameters (like grip strength, walking speed, or cognitive performance), or aging biomarkers (like chronic inflammation levels or epigenetic patterns). To understand this new industry fully, Social Capital partnered with a team of leading researchers to put together a two-part deep dive into longevity biotech and aging research. We recently released the part 2. Head to my Substack to read it: https://lnkd.in/gQZX6vN4

I’m excited to share that Mirai has raised $500,000 in pre-seed investment from a16z speedrun . When people look for a home, they’re not just buying the building. They’re buying the commute, the schools, and the neighborhood that will shape their lives. Yet nearly every real estate listing stops at the property line. We have sophisticated ways to experience a home online, but understanding the surrounding area still means piecing together information scattered across the internet. We’re building Mirai to change that. Mirai turns any address into a virtual neighborhood experience, helping buyers understand what living there could feel like before scheduling a showing. I’m incredibly grateful to be building this alongside Andrew Shum and Caleb Lo , with the support of Fareed Mosavat and Jonathan Lai . A huge thank you as well to the entire a16z speedrun team, including Andrew Chen , Joshua Lu , Kenan Saleh , Marcus Segal , Troy Kirwin , Emily Bennett , Seeam Shahid Noor , Samira Behrouzan , Macy Mills , Lester Chen , Tom Hammer , Lejla Johnsen , Andrew Lee , Jordan Mazer , Jordan Carver , Bella Nazzari , Joe G. ri, Joe G., Marigold Vu , Jacqueline Young , Joan DeGennaro and everyone else who has helped sharpen our thinking and will help us move this vision forward. And thank you to Musa Aqeel , Peter Bai , and Fahmi Omer for supporting us from the earliest stages. We’re opening private-beta partnerships with agents, brokerages, and builders, and hiring across engineering, product, and go-to-market. The most common question we got after publishing our work with CMS: how do you know 100,000+ extracted business rules are accurate? The answer has two parts: expert graders and a citation trail. CMS subject-matter experts graded randomly sampled rules against their own knowledge of the systems. A few of them were in the room when the original COBOL was written. Every rule carries its evidence: the source lines it came from, or the CMS documentation that confirms it. 18M+ lines of Assembly and COBOL is too much for any team to re-read. The grading and the citations make the record checkable. Read more: https://lnkd.in/gBTtqz2s

Probably an overshare, but I've been wanting to talk a little bit about my move to Tesla now that my 90 day mark has passed and my career goals. When I moved to this team, one of the things that I was changing was the genre of students I'd get to work with! In my previous lives, a majority of my ecosystem and comfort zone was recruiting and working with students in a technical capacity! From software engineers to machine learning, product managers to science, a majority of my career as a recruiter was built working in this space. tbh, I was pretty anxious and felt overwhelmed by technical jargon and the landscape of it all - but over time, I found comfort. Call it brute force, but I became comfortable reviewing resumes. I became comfortable speaking in public. I loved attending hackathons like nwPlus and Hack the North , loved learning about the diversity of projects and tech stacks that existed out there. I got to partner with schools with caring staff. Managers were really educational. Engineers were super understanding. And the students were so, so, kind. It became easier to talk with them. I didn't feel out of place. No one judged me. I was in my own head. That anxiousness eventually was replaced with both warmth, and comfort. At the same time, there was a trade-off that was happening. I did feel that there many students that didn't feel represented or heard. As the world tends to remind me, it's a huge, huge place. And where I was more available/accessible in one space, I was a stranger to many others. So when the opportunity made the most sense, I left the comfort of being in a technical space, to pursue recruiting in a new sector. For those who don't know, I now focus on internships in the Manufacturing space! I work with students from Manufacturing, Mechanical, Industrial, and Design backgrounds, and a more traditional genre of engineering altogether now. In many ways, I am that anxious person again but in many more ways, I am learning all over again. And because of this, I'm able to help more students than before. I don't get to talk much about career goals, but I do not yearn to be a recruiter that specializes in a certain sector - I yearn to be a recruiter that specializes in students. Comprehensively, in every space. Because it isn't a specific sector that I find comfort in, it is working with students that makes it so rewarding c: I'm in a really unique position, and I am aware of that! I am able to do both. So you'll see postings from me about my engineering roles and once in a blue moon, you'll see postings from me for technical roles too! My skip fondly referred to this as being a swiss army knife. I refer to this as being really, really, lucky. I yearn to be agnostic. I want to learn it all. That's what makes it a mighty goal. My career has always been in greater service to students and with this, I am able to do so for a larger, larger, population. --- ps: i'd love to recruit ux someday c:

I'm wrapping up my internship at Scotiabank a little earlier than expected. But before I share what's next, I wanted to reflect on few things I've learned over the past seven months. When I switched majors in my third year of university, I felt like I was behind everyone else. I graduated a semester later than most of my friends, wondering if I was already "late". When I joined the bank as a CX Design Intern in January, I wasn't even sure if I had the skills to do well in my role. I didn't study design. Honestly, I didn't even know what CX was before January. Looking back, I realize I was worrying about the wrong things. 💡 One thing that changed everything for me was simply 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬. Since I didn't come from a design background, I reached out to UX designers, service designers, and product designers because I was genuinely curious about their work and wanted to understand how they made their design decisions. Beyond designers, I talked to anyone who was willing to share their experiences. Every person around you has experiences that you can learn from. If you're an intern or just starting your career, don't be afraid of not knowing things. Nobody expects you to know everything. You're new to the company, to the industry, maybe even to corporate life itself. People are usually more than happy to help if they see that you're genuinely curious and willing to learn. 💡 Another thing I learned is to 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐰𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮. If you have capacity (and most interns probably do), ask if there's something you can help with. I looked for ways I could contribute instead of waiting for someone to assign me work. It might start with something small, but if you do it well, people remember and start trusting you with bigger projects, more responsibility, and opportunities you never expected you would have as an intern. That could feel overwhelming sometimes, and there were definitely moments where I looked at my backlog and thought, "Can I actually do this?" But one quote has really stuck with me: "𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐞." If people keep trusting you with bigger opportunities, it's because they believe you're capable. It pushes you to learn faster, think differently, and grow in ways you probably wouldn't if you stayed comfortable. So 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞. 💡 One last thing I want to share is this from our EVP: 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐬. I wasn't chasing a specific title or trying to fit into the "perfect role". I wanted to become someone who create compelling designs, communicate ideas clearly, take ownership, collaborate across teams, challenge ideas respectfully, and be someone others could rely on. Over time, those small things started adding up. People trusted me with bigger initiatives, asking for my input, and giving me opportunities I never expected to have as an intern. The titles will come. The skills are what stay with you. And that's why I'm wrapping up my internship a little earlier than expected - I'm excited to be continuing my journey at Scotiabank as a Manager, CX Programs & Visual Design. I know it's a big jump, but to me, it reflects my team's belief in my potential. Now it's my turn to stretch, grow, and live up to that trust. So if you're feeling behind or don't feel "qualified enough", don't let that stop you. Be curious. Ask questions. Take initiative. Learn from the people around you. None of this would've been possible without my team - Natasha Mohindra , Andrea Erickson (Huitrón) , Nick Somwaru, Julia Cipollone (Soye) , and everyone in the Client Expereince Management Office and the program.🚀 Thank you for trusting me with meaningful work and creating an environment where I could learn, make mistakes, and grow. I couldn't have asked for a better team to start my career with. Looking forward to this next chapter! ❤️
